title: Chasing Stolen Wealth Across Borders
paras: When a public official diverts money from a state treasury, the theft is only the first stage of a longer problem. Funds taken from school, hospital or road budgets rarely stay where they were stolen. They are moved, often within days, through a chain of accounts, companies and properties in several jurisdictions, so that by the time an investigation begins the trail may cross five or six borders. Recovering those assets, rather than merely convicting the thief, has therefore become a distinct and demanding branch of law enforcement, one that tests the cooperation of states that have little else in common.

The first obstacle is concealment. Those who launder stolen funds seldom hold them in their own names. Instead they rely on shell companies, which exist on paper only, and on nominees, ordinary individuals who agree to appear as the owners of record. A single villa on a foreign coast may belong to a company registered in one territory, itself owned by a trust in another, whose beneficiaries are recorded in neither. Investigators must peel back each layer, and each layer may lie within the legal reach of a different state that has no obligation to help. Registers of beneficial ownership, which list the real people who ultimately control a company, were designed to shorten this task, but their value depends on whether the information is verified and on who is permitted to read it.

The second obstacle is legal. The traditional route is mutual legal assistance, in which one state asks another to gather evidence or freeze property. Requests must satisfy the formal requirements of the receiving country, are often translated, and may take years to answer. Meanwhile the money can be moved again. Many jurisdictions also insist on a criminal conviction before assets can be confiscated, which is impossible if the suspect has died, fled or remains in power. Some countries have therefore developed non-conviction-based forfeiture, which targets the property rather than the person and requires a court to be persuaded only that the assets probably derive from crime. Supporters regard this as a pragmatic remedy; critics warn that it lowers the standard of proof against owners who have not been found guilty of anything.

A third difficulty concerns what happens once the money is recovered. Returning funds to a government that was itself implicated in their theft would seem to defeat the purpose of the exercise. Several recent arrangements have therefore placed recovered sums under independent supervision, directing them towards projects that civil society groups can monitor, such as vaccination programmes or rural electrification. Such conditions are sometimes denounced as an affront to sovereignty, since they imply that the victim state cannot be trusted with its own property. Defenders reply that sovereignty belongs to a country's citizens, not to whoever happens to control its treasury at a given moment.

Practitioners disagree about where the greatest improvement lies. One camp argues that the priority is prevention: transparent public procurement, asset declarations by officials and prompt reporting of suspicious transactions by banks make large thefts harder to hide in the first place. A second camp contends that prevention, however admirable, does nothing for the sums already abroad, and that investment should go into specialist units able to follow money in real time. The two positions are less opposed than they sound, since the data produced by preventive systems is precisely what such units need, but budgets are finite and the emphasis a government chooses reveals a good deal about what it actually wants.

Technology has complicated rather than simplified the picture. Analytical software can scan millions of transactions for patterns that a human clerk would miss, and leaked archives have occasionally exposed entire networks. Yet digital currencies allow value to cross borders in minutes without passing through a regulated bank, and some are designed to obscure the sender. It would be a mistake, however, to assume that criminals hold the advantage. Public blockchains keep a permanent record, and several seizures have succeeded precisely because a transaction made years earlier could be reconstructed.

What emerges is a picture of partial progress. Recovery rates remain low in comparison with the amounts believed to have been stolen, and the process is slow, costly and uncertain. Nevertheless, each completed case establishes precedents and trains investigators, while the growing expectation that stolen wealth can be pursued may alter the calculations of those who contemplate theft. The deterrent effect, which is difficult to measure, may ultimately matter more than the sums returned.

sumAr: يشرح النص صعوبات تتبع الأموال العامة المسروقة عبر الحدود، من إخفاء الملكية والعقبات القانونية إلى مصير الأموال المستردة. ويخلص إلى أن التقدم جزئي، وأن أثر الردع قد يكون أهم من المبالغ المستردة.

title: Can Scientific Results Be Repeated?
paras: In recent years, a series of attempts to repeat published experiments has unsettled several fields. Teams of researchers, working independently, set out to re-run studies whose findings had been widely cited, and in a troubling proportion of cases they obtained smaller effects or none at all. The phrase reproducibility crisis entered the vocabulary, and it has been used so freely that its meaning has blurred. Before asking how serious the problem is, it is worth establishing what a failure to reproduce actually shows.

The first step is to separate two ideas that are often confused. A result is reproducible when another analyst, given the same data and the same code, arrives at the same numbers. It is replicable when a fresh study, with new participants or materials, finds the same pattern. A failed replication does not automatically mean that the original claim was false. The new sample may differ in age, culture or season; the equipment may be calibrated differently; a crucial condition may have gone unrecorded. Equally, a successful replication can mislead if both studies share the same hidden flaw. The evidence is informative, but it is never a verdict. Careful researchers therefore report exactly how a repetition differed from the original.

Why, then, do so many published findings fail to hold? Statistical weakness is the most frequently cited cause. Studies with small samples produce unstable estimates, and researchers who test many hypotheses on the same data will find some patterns that look significant purely by chance. The problem is aggravated by the habits of publication. Journals prefer novel, positive results, so experiments that show no effect often remain unpublished, a phenomenon known as the file-drawer problem. Researchers respond rationally to incentives: careers advance on the number of striking papers produced, not on the number of careful checks carried out.

Reformers have proposed a range of remedies. Under pre-registration, a team states its hypotheses and its analysis plan before collecting any data, which removes the temptation to adjust the analysis once results appear. In the format known as registered reports, a journal agrees to publish a paper on the strength of its method before the results are known, so that a null finding is as publishable as a dramatic one. Others emphasise open data and shared code, allowing anyone to check the calculations, and large collaborative projects in which many laboratories run the same protocol. Early signs suggest that such measures raise the proportion of findings that survive repetition.

These reforms have their critics, who raise objections more subtle than simple resistance to change. Rigid pre-registration, they argue, can discourage exploratory work, in which unexpected patterns suggest new questions; some of the most productive discoveries began as surprises. The administrative burden also falls unevenly, penalising small teams without technical support. Above all, a single standard may not suit every discipline. A laboratory experiment can be run again next week, but a survey of a rare habitat, or an observation of an unrepeatable astronomical event, cannot. Demanding identical repetition in such fields misunderstands what their evidence is.

A more optimistic reading holds that the whole episode demonstrates science working as intended, since the problem was detected by scientists themselves. There is truth in this, but it should not be pressed too far. Self-correction is neither automatic nor quick. Weak findings can persist for decades in textbooks, and in medicine or education they may shape practice long before anyone checks them. Correction happens only when someone is paid, praised or at least permitted to do the checking, and that is a matter of institutional design rather than of scientific character.

Perhaps the most useful lesson is therefore a modest one. The goal should not be perfect reproducibility, which no empirical field has ever possessed, but calibrated confidence: a habit of treating any single study as provisional, reporting uncertainty openly, and giving weight to results that several independent teams have obtained. Achieving that habit will require funders and universities to reward verification as generously as they now reward discovery.

qs.q: A failed replication does not necessarily prove that the original study was wrong.
qs.why: الفقرة 2: الفشل لا يعني تلقائياً أن الادعاء الأصلي خاطئ.

sumAr: يميّز النص بين إعادة إنتاج النتائج وتكرار الدراسات، ويعرض أسباب ضعف بعض النتائج المنشورة والإصلاحات المقترحة والانتقادات الموجهة إليها. ويخلص إلى أن الهدف هو ثقة معايَرة بالنتائج، تدعمها حوافز تكافئ التحقق.

title: Opening the Black Box: Explainable AI
paras: Automated systems now help to decide who receives a loan, which job applicants are interviewed and which patients are treated first. Many of the most accurate of these systems are built from layers of mathematical operations so numerous that even their designers cannot say, in ordinary language, why a particular input produced a particular output. Such models are commonly called black boxes. The field of explainable artificial intelligence has grown up in response, with the aim of making the reasoning of automated systems intelligible to the people who depend on them or are affected by them.

Three motives drive the field, and they do not always coincide. The first is accountability. A person refused a mortgage has a reasonable claim to know why, and a legal right to contest a decision is worthless if nobody can say what the decision rested on. The second is debugging. Explanations can reveal that a model has learned a shortcut: a program trained to recognise skin disease, for example, might have quietly learned to treat the presence of a ruler in the photograph as a sign of illness, because doctors tended to measure the worrying cases. The third is trust, though this is the most slippery of the three, for trust that is not earned by good performance is merely a feeling.

Broadly, two strategies exist. The first is to use models that are interpretable by design, such as short decision lists or scoring tables that a person can read from top to bottom. The second is to keep a complex model and add a post hoc explanation, a separate technique that highlights which parts of the input mattered most, or that states a counterfactual, such as the claim that the loan would have been approved had the applicant's income been somewhat higher. Counterfactuals are especially popular because they tell the affected person what could be done differently.

Sceptics point out a weakness in the second strategy. A post hoc explanation is itself a model of the original model, and it may describe its behaviour inaccurately. An explanation can be persuasive without being faithful, offering a tidy story that has little to do with the real computation. In high-stakes settings such as criminal justice or medicine, this critique concludes, we should not try to explain black boxes at all but should avoid them, relying on transparent models whose workings can be audited directly.

Defenders of complex models answer that the premise of this argument, that simpler models are nearly as accurate, holds for some kinds of data but not for others. With images, speech and free text, deep models outperform simple ones by a wide margin, and insisting on simplicity could cost lives in diagnosis. Still, the sceptics have a point that is often overlooked: for the structured, tabular data that dominates lending and administration, carefully designed simple models frequently come close to their complex rivals, which suggests that the supposed trade-off between accuracy and interpretability is sometimes exaggerated.

A further complication lies with the human recipient. An explanation is addressed to someone, and what satisfies a regulator will not help a patient. Experimental studies have found that people may place more confidence in a system that supplies reasons, even when the reasons are flawed. If so, explanation can make users less critical rather than more, the opposite of what was intended. The design of explanations therefore needs the methods of psychology as much as those of computer science. An explanation tested only on its authors, rather than on its intended readers, tells us very little about whether it works.

It follows that explanation should never be treated as a substitute for testing. Whatever technique is used, systems that affect people's lives still need independent audits, monitoring of their real-world outcomes and routes of appeal. The most productive question is perhaps not whether a model can be explained but what a particular explanation is for, who will read it, and what they will be able to do with it.

sumAr: يناقش النص مسعى جعل قرارات الذكاء الاصطناعي مفهومة، ودوافعه وطرقه، ثم انتقادات التفسير اللاحق وحجج المدافعين عن النماذج المعقدة. ويخلص إلى أن التفسير لا يغني عن الاختبار والتدقيق المستقل.
